Based on my research, the evidence doesn't clearly support "yes" — the honest answer is "uncertain/mixed."

## What the Evidence Shows

**The most rigorous evidence is inconclusive.** The Cochrane Collaboration's systematic review of hypnotherapy for smoking cessation (Barnes et al., 2019, updated from 2010) — the gold-standard synthesis of randomized controlled trials — concluded that evidence is **insufficient** to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective than other treatments or no treatment at all, due to small sample sizes, high risk of bias, and heterogeneous methods across trials ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12519978_Hypnotherapy_for_smoking_cessation_Cochrane_Review); [hypnosiscredentials.com](https://hypnosiscredentials.com/hypnosis/research/hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/)). A 2021 Cochrane umbrella review reaffirmed this uncertainty ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full)).

**However, some individual trials show promise.** At least one RCT found hypnotherapy more effective than nicotine replacement therapy for cessation ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260373404_Hypnotherapy_is_more_effective_than_nicotine_replacement_therapy_for_smoking_cessation_Results_of_a_randomized_controlled_trial)), and a broader 2025 systematic review by Ekanayake & Elkins examining 63 studies (1968–2022) found that roughly two-thirds reported a positive effect of hypnosis on quitting smoking ([ishhypnosis.org](https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/)). This suggests a trend toward benefit, though it's a lower bar of evidence than the Cochrane standard.

**Official guidance is cautious.** The NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes hypnotherapy is used for smoking cessation but does not endorse it as a proven first-line approach, distinguishing it from conventional treatments (counseling, medication) that have well-established efficacy ([nccih.nih.gov](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/complementary-health-approaches-for-smoking-cessation)).

## Bottom Line

The claim that hypnosis "helps" isn't clearly false, but it's not firmly established either. Individual studies and a recent broad review lean positive, but the highest-quality evidence synthesis (Cochrane) says we can't yet confirm hypnotherapy outperforms other quit methods. It may help some people, particularly combined with other strategies, but shouldn't be relied on as a standalone, proven solution.
